state.case_summary:
A 63-year-old man presented with an 8-month history of painless scrotal swelling. Physical examination revealed bilateral testicular enlargement without tenderness. Scrotal ultrasound showed large, solid masses in both testes. Serum β-human chorionic gonadotropin, α-fetoprotein, and lactate dehydrogenase were all within normal limits. To evaluate for lymphoid malignancy, a positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan was performed and showed no evidence of lymphadenopathy or extranodal lymphomatous masses. After multidisciplinary discussion, a left radical inguinal orchiectomy was performed. The specimen contained a 7.0 × 6.0 × 4.2 cm tumor confined to the testis with lymphovascular invasion. Histologic examination demonstrated a pleomorphic tumor composed of three distinct cell types: small cells, medium cells, and large cells.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. spermatocytic seminoma
B. Testicular lymphoma was considered given the patient’s age and presentation
C. Germ cell tumor was included in the initial differential but tumor markers were normal
D. Leukemia was part of the differential diagnosis
E. Granulomatous inflammation was also considered
F. Lymphoma was effectively excluded by imaging that showed no nodal or extranodal involvement
G. Spermatocytic seminoma was diagnosed based on the classic histopathology of three cell sizes
H. None
